questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that an NFR without a planned measurement approach "is just an opinion with a number attached"?
options: Because without a way to actually check whether the target was met, the NFR can never be verified as true or false, so it can't function as a real, enforceable requirement
Because numbers in NFRs are always inaccurate
Because Salesforce automatically measures every NFR without a test plan
Because measurement plans are only needed for compliance NFRs
questions.explain: A metric and target that nobody ever tests is unverifiable — it's written down, but there's no way to confirm it was actually achieved, which is exactly what separates a real, enforceable requirement from an unchecked assumption.

questions.q: Why might a performance NFR referencing a 15-million-record object be difficult to test meaningfully in a Developer sandbox?
options: Developer sandboxes cannot run Apex code at all
Performance testing is not possible in any sandbox type, only in production
Developer sandboxes are only available to Government Cloud customers

Different sandbox types hold different data volumes and refresh on different schedules, and a Developer sandbox typically holds only a small data sample, not enough to realistically simulate the specified volume
questions.explain: The test environment is part of the NFR's design — a Developer sandbox's limited data volume can't realistically simulate a 15-million-record scenario, so the test plan needs an environment (like a Full or Partial Copy sandbox) that can actually hold enough data.

questions.q: What does Salesforce's Security Health Check tool actually do, and what is its limitation per this lesson?
options: It fully tests record-level and field-level access against any custom NFR and requires no further verification

It scores an org's security settings against a Salesforce-defined baseline and flags shortfalls, but it covers org-wide settings and doesn't substitute for testing record-level and field-level access against an NFR's specific requirements
It is a Shield feature that encrypts data at rest
It automatically fixes any security misconfiguration it detects
questions.explain: Security Health Check is a useful first-pass scoring tool against a general baseline, but it doesn't test whether a specific profile sees or doesn't see specific data as a specific NFR requires — that needs direct access-control verification.

questions.q: What is "failure injection" as a testing technique for reliability NFRs?
options: Running the happy-path test repeatedly until it passes
A Salesforce governor-limit setting that injects random errors into production
Deliberately causing the specified failure condition (a timeout, a duplicate payload, a disconnected callout target) to verify that the system's specified response actually happens
A compliance audit technique used only for GDPR requirements
questions.explain: Failure injection deliberately triggers the failure scenario a reliability NFR describes — rather than only testing the happy path — to confirm the retry, idempotent write, or flag-for-review behavior actually works as specified.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does skipping NFR testing and relying on "we'll find out in production" actually cost?
options: It moves the discovery of whether the NFR was met from a controlled test environment, where a failure costs a bug ticket, to production, where the same failure costs real data, downtime, or a compliance violation discovered by a user or auditor
Nothing — NFRs are self-enforcing once written down
It only affects compliance NFRs, not performance or reliability NFRs
It guarantees the NFR will be met, since production is the most realistic environment
questions.explain: Skipping testing doesn't make an NFR true — it just shifts where the failure is discovered, from a cheap, controlled test environment to expensive, high-stakes production, discovered by the people the NFR was meant to protect rather than by a tester.
